title: The Wound That Teaches Date Published: June 4, 2026 Original URL: https://thelastanalogue.substack.com
author: Jonathan Boymal
summary: Boymal uses the Greek myth of Chiron — the immortal centaur who continued teaching heroes after being struck by an accidental poisoned arrow that could not heal — to reframe the question of AI and human teachers away from capability and toward irreplaceable wound-derived wisdom. Jung's 'wounded healer' archetype supplies the psychological mechanism: the therapist (or teacher) whose own unhealed depths make them permeable to others' suffering — the wound becomes a means of perception that cannot be simulated. The standard 'centaur' metaphor for human-AI collaboration (human judgment plus machine speed outperforms either alone) is useful but incomplete: it is a metaphor about capability. Boymal asks what the human half specifically contributes that requires having been wounded. A great teacher can offer genuine testimony — 'I was here once, in this exact confusion, and I know its shape from the inside' — and the student receives this not as information but as permission to remain in difficulty without catastrophizing it. AI can be trained to simulate this ('many students find this difficult'), but the simulation is, at best, a counterfeit narrative: AI has processed the textual shadow of confusion but has never lived the confusion as wound, and students can distinguish the genuine from the counterfeit in high-stakes moments. The Chiron myth's resolution — Chiron eventually chooses death, surrendering his immortality to free Prometheus, and Zeus places him among the stars — suggests that wound and wisdom are not permanent burdens but transformative materials, and that the teachers now navigating AI's disruption are living inside the long middle of an unfinished myth.
points: Boymal's key reframe is that the distinctive value of a human teacher is not pedagogical technique (which AI can replicate) but existential testimony — the ability to say, from genuine experience, 'I have been confused in exactly this way, and it did not destroy me,' which gives students permission to tolerate their own difficulty.

AI's fundamental limitation as a teacher is not its knowledge but its lack of wound: it has processed every description of confusion, failure, and breakthrough, but has not lived those states as stakes-laden experience, and therefore cannot provide what Boymal calls 'witness rather than information.'

The wounded-healer framework explains why the most effective teaching moments are often not the most technically skilled but the most personally honest — when a teacher makes their own history of struggle visible, it changes the student's relationship to difficulty.

Teachers who spent years helping students become fluent with technology are now facing a version of Chiron's wound: the skills they transmitted are now the force that questions their own value, a form of irony the myth captures precisely.

The Chiron ending — transformation rather than erasure — suggests a different relationship to the wound: not something to overcome but something to carry, work with, and eventually transmute into the kind of wisdom that requires having been struck.
quotes: Chiron, known in Greek mythology as the wisest and most just of all centaurs, had mastered medicine, music, mathematics, and the art of teaching heroes. One afternoon he was struck by a poisoned arrow. The arrow belonged to Heracles. It went astray in a skirmish with other centaurs, and wounded Chiron by accident.

As Chiron was immortal, the wound could not kill him. It also could not heal. So he continued. He taught Achilles the lyre and the spear. He trained Asclepius, who would become the god of medicine itself. All of this while carrying, somewhere beneath the surface, a wound that never closed.

Chiron complicates this. He asks: what does the human bring to the hybrid that only comes from having been wounded? What if the most important thing the human half of the centaur carries is the scars?

It has not been confused. It has not sat with a problem for three days and felt the specific humiliation of not understanding something that seems obvious to everyone else. It has not experienced the strange relief when comprehension finally arrives. It has processed those experiences as a textual shadow. It has not lived them as wound.

The great teacher in that moment can make visible their own history of being stuck. As genuine testimony: I was here once. This confusion you are in, I know its shape from the inside. The student receives this as permission. Permission to remain in difficulty without catastrophising it.

There is something in a human account of difficulty that generated language cannot replicate. Call it witness rather than information, dependent on something that is genuinely at stake for the teacher, something carried rather than computed.

Teachers are now living some version of this. Many of them have spent years helping students become fluent with technology, passing on whatever wisdom they had accumulated about how to learn in the age of screens. And now the rise of AI systems create a new kind of wound, in the form of questioning the value of the profession.
